column1: A function can assign the same output to two different inputs.|T|For example, squaring 2 and −2 gives 4. Each input still has exactly one output.
The domain of a real-valued function includes every real number automatically.|F|The domain excludes inputs where the rule is undefined, such as division by zero.
For f(x) = x², f(−3) = −9.|F|Squaring means multiplying −3 by −3, giving positive 9.
The graph of y = f(x) + 2 is shifted upward by 2.|T|Every output increases by 2 while the input stays the same.
The graph of y = f(x − 2) is shifted left by 2.|F|The same output occurs at an input 2 larger, so the shift is to the right.
An even function satisfies f(−x) = f(x).|T|Its graph is symmetric about the vertical axis wherever both inputs are in the domain.
An inverse function reverses the input-output relationship.|T|If f(a) = b, its inverse sends b back to a on the chosen domain.
Every function has an inverse function without restricting its domain.|F|An inverse function requires one-to-one behavior. Squaring on all real numbers fails this requirement.
In f(g(2)), evaluate g at 2 before applying f.|T|Composition uses the output of the inner function as the input to the outer function.
A limit can exist at a point where the function is undefined.|T|A limit describes nearby behavior; the value at the point itself is a separate matter.
Equal finite left-hand and right-hand limits give the two-sided limit.|T|Approaching from both sides must lead to the same value.
Continuity at a requires the limit at a to equal f(a).|T|The function must be defined there, the limit must exist, and the two values must agree.
A continuous function must be differentiable everywhere.|F|The absolute-value function is continuous at zero but has a sharp corner there.
If f is differentiable at a, it is continuous at a.|T|A finite derivative implies the function approaches its value smoothly enough to be continuous.
For f(x) = x², the tangent slope at x = 3 is 6.|T|The derivative is 2x; substituting 3 gives 6.
Average velocity over an interval is its final position divided by elapsed time.|F|Use displacement, final position minus initial position, divided by elapsed time.
A derivative can be negative.|T|A negative derivative means the output decreases locally as the input increases.
The derivative of a constant function is that constant.|F|A constant function does not change, so its derivative is zero.
The derivative of x⁵ is 5x⁴.|T|The power rule multiplies by the exponent and then lowers it by one.
The derivative of sin x is cos x when x is measured in radians.|T|The standard trigonometric derivative formulas use radian measure.
The derivative of eˣ is xeˣ⁻¹.|F|The exponential eˣ is its own derivative; the ordinary power rule does not apply to a variable exponent.
The derivative of ln x is defined for x > 0 in real calculus.|T|The real logarithm ln x has positive domain, and its derivative there is the reciprocal of x.
Differentiating sin(x²) requires multiplying by 2x.|T|The chain rule includes the derivative of the inner function x².
The derivative of a quotient is always the quotient of the derivatives.|F|The quotient rule combines the original functions and derivatives and divides by the denominator squared.
Implicit differentiation treats y as a function of x.|T|Differentiating a term containing y requires the chain rule and a factor of y′.
For x² + y² = 1, differentiation gives 2x + 2y y′ = 0.|T|Both squared terms are differentiated, and y² contributes its inner derivative y′.
A related-rates equation can mix meters and centimeters without conversion.|F|Use compatible units before substituting rates and lengths into the same relationship.
A zero derivative guarantees a local maximum.|F|The function x³ has zero derivative at zero but no local maximum there.
A critical number can occur where the derivative does not exist but the function does.|T|Critical numbers include points in the domain with zero or undefined derivative.
A positive second derivative throughout an interval indicates concavity upward.|T|The slope is increasing there, which makes the graph bend upward.
An inflection point requires a change in concavity.|T|A zero second derivative alone is not sufficient; check how concavity changes across the point.
The Mean Value Theorem requires continuity on the closed interval and differentiability inside it.|T|Under those conditions some tangent slope equals the overall secant slope.
A continuous function on a closed bounded interval attains its absolute extrema.|T|The Extreme Value Theorem guarantees both a maximum and a minimum under these assumptions.
An optimization problem never requires checking endpoints.|F|An absolute maximum or minimum on a restricted interval may occur at an endpoint.
L’Hôpital’s rule applies directly to every quotient limit.|F|It requires an eligible indeterminate form and derivative-limit conditions, not just any quotient.
A linear approximation uses the tangent line near its base point.|T|The approximation uses the function value and derivative at that point; accuracy usually worsens farther away.
Reversing the limits of a definite integral changes its sign.|T|The orientation of accumulation reverses, so the integral is negated.
The definite integral of a nonnegative continuous function can be negative when the lower limit is smaller.|F|With the usual increasing orientation, all accumulated contributions are nonnegative.
Every antiderivative of x on an interval differs from x² divided by 2 by a constant.|T|Functions with the same derivative on an interval differ by a constant.
A Riemann sum multiplies each sample value by a subinterval width.|T|Each term approximates the contribution of a narrow strip.
A definite integral always represents unsigned geometric area.|F|Parts below the horizontal axis contribute negatively to a signed integral.
If F′ = f and f is continuous, the integral from a to b is F(b) − F(a).|T|This is the evaluation form of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
The integral over an interval of zero width is zero.|T|There is no interval over which to accumulate contributions.
Substitution in a definite integral leaves the bounds unchanged automatically.|F|When switching variables, transform the bounds too, or return to the original variable before evaluating.
The average value of a continuous function on [a,b] is its integral divided by b − a.|T|This divides the total accumulation by the interval length, assuming b is greater than a.
Area between two curves can require splitting the interval where the curves cross.|T|The upper and lower curves can exchange roles at an intersection.
The disk method uses cross-sectional area perpendicular to the axis of rotation.|T|A disk contributes its circular area times a small thickness along the axis.
A washer has area π times the difference of the squared outer and inner radii.|T|Subtract the inner disk area from the outer disk area.
The shell method uses only the radius and ignores shell height.|F|A thin shell volume includes circumference, height, and thickness.
Rotating a region around a horizontal axis always requires integrating with respect to x.|F|Both x and y methods may work; the chosen slices determine disks, washers, or shells.
Work done by a varying force along a line is found by integrating the force over displacement.|T|Each small displacement contributes force times displacement, with the correct sign.
Stretching an ideal Hooke’s-law spring twice as far requires twice as much work from equilibrium.|F|Force increases with stretch, so the work from equilibrium is proportional to the stretch squared.
A slice-based volume integral must account for any change in cross-sectional area.|T|The area can vary along the solid and belongs inside the integral.
Mass equals density times volume only when density is uniform throughout the object.|T|For varying density, integrate density over the volume rather than using one local value.
Integration by parts comes from the product rule.|T|Integrating the product-rule identity and rearranging gives the integration-by-parts formula.
A trigonometric substitution can simplify certain square-root expressions.|T|Identities such as one minus sine squared equals cosine squared help remove a root.
Partial fractions decompose a suitable rational function into simpler fractions.|T|Factor the denominator and use forms appropriate to its linear or irreducible quadratic factors.
An improper integral is evaluated using a limit.|T|Infinite bounds or unbounded integrands require checking a limiting accumulation.
An infinite integration interval guarantees an infinite integral.|F|Some functions decay fast enough to have a finite integral over an infinite interval.
The integral of 1 over x from 1 to infinity converges.|F|Its antiderivative is ln x, which grows without bound as the upper limit increases.
The integral of 1 over x² from 1 to infinity converges.|T|Its limiting accumulation is 1, because the reciprocal of the upper limit tends to zero.
A numerical integration approximation is automatically exact.|F|Trapezoidal and Simpson approximations generally have errors unless special exactness conditions hold.

A rational integrand with numerator degree at least denominator degree may need polynomial division first.|T|Division separates a polynomial part and a proper rational fraction before partial fractions.
Arc length adds lengths of small pieces rather than signed vertical changes.|T|Length is nonnegative and accumulates along the path.
For a smooth graph y = f(x), arc length uses the square root of 1 + f′(x)².|T|The formula comes from the Pythagorean length of a short horizontal and vertical displacement.
A horizontal segment of width 4 has arc length zero.|F|Its slope is zero, but the segment still has horizontal length 4.
Surface area of revolution depends on distance from the rotation axis.|T|Each narrow strip sweeps a circumference determined by its radius.
Hydrostatic pressure in a stationary uniform-density liquid increases with depth.|T|The weight of the liquid above produces a pressure increase proportional to depth.
A deeper horizontal strip of a vertical submerged plate generally experiences greater pressure.|T|Pressure varies with depth, so force on the plate is integrated over its area.
The centroid of a uniform symmetric region lies on its axis of symmetry.|T|Equal contributions on opposite sides balance their first moments about that axis.
A probability density can be negative on a small interval.|F|A probability density is nonnegative; integrating it gives nonnegative probabilities.
The total integral of a probability density over its domain is 1.|T|The entire possible outcome range must have total probability one.
A differential equation describes a relationship involving an unknown function and its derivatives.|T|Its solutions are functions whose values and derivatives satisfy the relationship.
A direction field assigns a local slope to each point where the differential equation is defined.|T|A solution curve follows those local directions.
For y′ = y, every curve y = Ceˣ satisfies the equation.|T|Differentiating Ceˣ produces the same expression Ceˣ.
An initial condition must be ignored when finding a particular solution.|F|The initial condition selects the member of the solution family that fits the starting data.
Separating variables may lose equilibrium solutions if you divide by a factor that can be zero.|T|Check the zero-factor cases separately before dividing.
Exponential growth with positive rate has a constant absolute increase per unit time.|F|Its rate is proportional to the current amount, so equal time intervals give equal multiplication factors.
In logistic growth with positive carrying capacity, the growth rate vanishes at the carrying capacity.|T|The limiting factor becomes zero when the population equals that capacity.
Euler’s method uses local slope information to estimate a nearby solution value.|T|It advances along a tangent approximation rather than solving the equation exactly.
A smaller Euler step always eliminates all numerical error.|F|Smaller steps often improve accuracy, but finite-step and rounding errors can remain.
A parametric curve gives coordinates as functions of a shared parameter.|T|The parameter links the horizontal and vertical positions along the curve.
Two different parameter values can correspond to the same point.|T|A curve can revisit a point, as happens on a closed path.
A vertical tangent may occur when the x derivative is zero and the y derivative is nonzero.|T|The horizontal motion stops instantaneously while the vertical motion remains nonzero.
For x = t and y = t², the slope at t = 2 is 4.|T|Divide the y derivative 2t by the x derivative 1.
A negative polar radius is always invalid.|F|It locates a point in the opposite direction from the stated angle.
Adding a full turn to a polar angle gives a different point when the radius is unchanged.|F|An angle increased by 2π points along the same ray.
A polar-area integral uses the square of the radius.|T|A thin sector has area approximately one-half radius squared times its angle width.
A curve’s geometric shape always specifies how quickly a particle moves along it.|F|Different parametrizations can trace the same shape with different speeds.
Eliminating a parameter can lose information about direction of travel.|T|The resulting coordinate equation describes the path but not necessarily its orientation or timing.
If a series converges, its terms approach zero.|T|The terms are differences between successive partial sums, which approach the same limit.
Terms approaching zero guarantee that their series converges.|F|The harmonic series has terms approaching zero but divergent partial sums.
An infinite geometric series with common ratio of magnitude less than 1 converges.|T|Its powers shrink fast enough that partial sums approach a finite limit.
An alternating series with decreasing positive term magnitudes approaching zero converges.|T|These are the conditions of the Alternating Series Test.
Absolute convergence implies convergence.|T|Convergence of the series of absolute values is strong enough to ensure the original series converges.
The ratio test settles convergence when its limiting ratio equals 1.|F|At a limit of 1 the ratio test is inconclusive; another test is needed.
A power series can require separate checks at its interval endpoints.|T|The ratio test typically gives the interior radius; each boundary can behave differently.
A Taylor polynomial uses derivatives at a chosen center.|T|Its coefficients match the function’s successive derivatives at that point.
A convergent sequence and a convergent series mean the same thing.|F|A sequence concerns its individual terms; a series concerns the partial sums of terms.
A vector has both magnitude and direction.|T|Its components describe directed displacements or other directed quantities.
The dot product of two vectors is a vector.|F|The dot product is a scalar, obtained by adding products of matching components.
The cross product of two three-dimensional vectors is perpendicular to both when it is nonzero.|T|Its direction follows the right-hand rule and is normal to their plane.
Parallel nonzero vectors have zero cross product.|T|The cross-product magnitude includes the sine of their angle, which is zero for parallel directions.
A unit vector has magnitude 1.|T|Normalizing a nonzero vector divides it by its magnitude.
The zero vector can be normalized by dividing by its length.|F|Its length is zero, and division by zero is undefined.
A plane can be described by a point and a nonzero normal vector.|T|The normal specifies the plane’s orientation, and the point fixes its position.
The angle between nonzero vectors can be found from their dot product and magnitudes.|T|The dot product equals the product of the magnitudes times the angle’s cosine.
A sphere of radius r consists of all points whose distance from its center equals r.|T|The sum of squared coordinate differences is r squared.
The derivative of a vector-valued position function is velocity.|T|Differentiate its coordinate functions to obtain the velocity components.
Speed equals the magnitude of velocity.|T|Speed is nonnegative and does not include the direction of motion.
Constant speed guarantees zero acceleration.|F|Acceleration can change velocity’s direction, as in uniform circular motion.
A tangent vector indicates the local direction of a smooth curve.|T|A nonzero derivative points in the direction of increasing parameter.
Acceleration is the second derivative of position with respect to time.|T|It is the rate of change of velocity.
Curvature measures how rapidly the tangent direction changes with distance along a curve.|T|Sharper bending means greater curvature.
A straight line has nonzero curvature everywhere.|F|Its tangent direction is constant, so its curvature is zero.
Tangential acceleration changes speed.|T|The tangential component is the derivative of speed with respect to time.
Normal acceleration points along the tangent direction.|F|It is perpendicular to the tangent and accounts for changing velocity direction.
A partial derivative holds the other independent variables constant.|T|It measures sensitivity to one variable at a time.
For f(x,y) = x²y, the partial derivative with respect to x is 2xy.|T|Treat y as a constant multiplier while differentiating x².
The gradient of a differentiable scalar field is a scalar.|F|The gradient is a vector of partial derivatives.
At a point with nonzero gradient, the gradient gives the direction of greatest local increase.|T|For unit directions, the directional derivative is largest in the gradient direction.
A zero gradient guarantees a local minimum.|F|A critical point can be a maximum, a minimum, or a saddle point.
A saddle point can increase in one direction and decrease in another.|T|Opposite local behavior prevents it from being a local maximum or minimum.
The multivariable chain rule accounts for every relevant path of dependence.|T|Changes can reach the output through more than one intermediate variable.
Lagrange multipliers can help locate extrema subject to a smooth constraint.|T|At regular constrained extrema, the objective gradient aligns with the constraint gradient.
Mixed second partial derivatives are always equal without any regularity conditions.|F|Their equality is guaranteed under suitable continuity conditions, not for every function.
A double integral can add contributions over a two-dimensional region.|T|Small area elements replace the intervals used in a single integral.
Changing integration order may require describing the same region with different bounds.|T|Horizontal and vertical slices can have different endpoint functions.
In polar coordinates, the area element is simply dr dθ.|F|The area element includes a factor r because angular strips widen with radius.
In cylindrical coordinates, the volume element includes a factor r.|T|The polar area scaling remains when a vertical thickness is added.
A triple integral of density over volume gives mass.|T|Each small piece contributes its density times its volume.
The Jacobian accounts for local area or volume scaling in a change of variables.|T|Its absolute determinant converts small pieces between coordinate systems.
A double integral of 1 over a region gives its area.|T|Each area element is counted with unit weight.
A negative density is appropriate for the mass density of an ordinary material.|F|Ordinary mass density is nonnegative; signed quantities require a different physical interpretation.
The bounds of a multiple integral should reflect the actual geometric region.|T|Wrong bounds integrate over a different set even when the integrand is correct.
A vector field assigns a vector to each point in its domain.|T|It can model velocity, force, or another directed quantity throughout a region.
A scalar line integral of density along a wire can give its mass.|T|Density per unit length is integrated against arc length.
Work along a path uses the component of force along the path displacement.|T|The force-displacement dot product keeps only the contributing component.
A conservative field has path-independent work between endpoints in its domain.|T|A potential function makes the line integral equal to the potential difference.
Every field with zero curl is globally conservative regardless of its domain.|F|Domain conditions matter; holes can prevent a single-valued potential even when curl vanishes.
Divergence measures local net outward flow per unit volume.|T|It compares how much field flows out of a tiny region with how much flows in.
Reversing a surface orientation reverses signed flux.|T|The unit normal changes sign, which negates its dot product with the field.
Stokes’ theorem relates surface curl to circulation around the boundary.|T|The boundary direction and surface normal must have compatible orientations.
The divergence theorem relates outward flux through a closed surface to a volume integral.|T|For a sufficiently smooth field, integrating divergence inside equals total outward flux.
A second-order equation contains a second derivative and no higher derivative.|T|Order is determined by the highest derivative appearing in the equation.
For y″ − y = 0, both eˣ and e⁻ˣ are solutions.|T|Each function has second derivative equal to itself.
A repeated characteristic root r requires only one solution eʳˣ for the full second-order solution.|F|A second independent solution is xeʳˣ, giving two arbitrary constants.
Complex conjugate characteristic roots can produce sine and cosine factors in real solutions.|T|Their real part gives an exponential envelope and their imaginary part sets the oscillation frequency.

For a nonhomogeneous linear equation, a particular solution can be added to the homogeneous general solution.|T|The homogeneous part contributes zero to the forcing, while the particular part produces it.
A positive damping force in a spring model supplies energy to sustain motion.|F|Ordinary damping opposes velocity and dissipates mechanical energy.
An undamped oscillator driven at its natural frequency can exhibit resonance.|T|In the ideal model, the forcing can add energy coherently and grow the oscillation amplitude.
A power-series method can seek a solution by matching coefficients of equal powers.|T|Substitution into the differential equation gives relations between the series coefficients.

Two arbitrary initial conditions always specify a solution even at a singular point of the equation.|F|Existence and uniqueness require suitable coefficient conditions, including a nonzero leading coefficient near the initial point.
